title: Fosas, fronteras y Palestina: las guerras contra la humanidad
content:
La segunda parte del recuento que hace Avispa Mídia del Semillero Guerra contra la humanidad. Las poblaciones y la naturaleza bajo asedio , convocado por el Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional (EZLN), aborda los crímenes contra la vida humana y la idea de “lo desechable” a través de distintas violencias contemporáneas desde el genocidio en Palestina, las desapariciones y asesinatos de personas en México, crímenes vinculadas a disputas territoriales y económicas; las condiciones que enfrentan las personas en desplazamiento forzado; y sobre los trabajadores frente a tecnologías emergentes y la precarización laboral.

La primera parte, la primera entrega, puedes leer aquí .

Durante estas sesiones el Capitán Insurgente Marcos destacó “la luz de resistencia y rebeldía de las madres buscadoras, a quienes, por mucho que las amemos, siempre les quedaremos a deber. Y que ahora nos impulsan a volver a caminar fuera de nuestras montañas, porque los brazos y los besos siempre es mejor darlos en persona y no por internet (...) y de forma especial, a las luchas, resistencias y rebeldías que han sido asediadas por siglos”.

Con la proyección de la pintura ¿Dónde estás, amor mío?, de Antonio Ramírez, basada en las madres buscadoras, la periodista y académica Alejandra Guillén habló de ‘Desaparición y leva para la acumulación de capital. Grietas de resistencia ante el nuevo dominio’.

“Es para ellas (madres buscadoras) también toda mi palabra y mucha de la que recojo viene de ellas, de sus hijos y de todas las personas que anónimamente hablan para explicar lo que está ocurriendo. Este es un saludo para las madres buscadoras que, lamentablemente, cada vez son más en este país”, dijo.

Recordó la historia de Jorge, ocurrida hace casi catorce años en Jiquilpan, en 2012, que coincide con el surgimiento del Cártel Jalisco Nueva Generación que desde sus inicios recurrió al reclutamiento forzado y al trabajo esclavo para conformar sus estructuras, una práctica que entonces aún no era reconocida como patrón de desaparición.

Las pistas reunidas por la familia, relató la periodista, ubicaban a Jorge en ranchos de la región de Tapalpa, un territorio que identificó como estratégico para la consolidación de la organización criminal y de economías legales e ilegales, como la explotación forestal y minera. En ese mismo periodo, añadió, también desaparecieron defensores del territorio en la Sierra de Manantlán, entre ellos Celedonio Monroy Prudencio, hubo el desplazamiento de comunidades enteras y el despojo sistemático de ranchos y tierras mediante las llamadas "limpias".

“Estaban sacando las maderas preciosas, las especies, las minas (...) Y lo han hecho, digamos, en alianza siempre con las mineras de la región. Y todo esto salía por los puertos, no solo en Jalisco, en toda la sierra de Jalisco y toda la sierra de Michoacán. Todo estaba ocurriendo al mismo tiempo”, precisó Alejandra Guillén.

Pero la expansión respondió a una estrategia previamente diseñada, articulada con rutas comerciales que permitían el intercambio de insumos para la producción de drogas sintéticas y otras mercancías provenientes de Asia.

La periodista hizo hincapié en que los grupos criminales en México constituyen apenas el nivel más visible de una red que involucra a actores financieros, políticos y empresariales. Entonces la violencia opera como parte de un modelo económico con objetivos de largo plazo, más que como una sucesión de hechos aislados.

En ese esquema, explicó que el reclutamiento forzado y la explotación de personas no solo sirven para conformar ejércitos, sino también para consolidar ese proyecto de expansión territorial basado en el control social y la transformación de quienes son sometidos.

En ese proceso buscan desarticular el tejido social, normalizar la crueldad e incorporar personas a un esquema de dominación que ha hecho posible ejercer un control permanente sobre barrios, pueblos y regiones.

“No es la primera vez que se esclaviza a personas, pero sí de la manera en que ha estado ocurriendo tan masivamente, decenas y decenas y decenas. Es como la fábrica del mal que instalaron, muy bien pensada, para no solo construir ejércitos, sino también transformar subjetividades (...) Y esta maquinaria ha necesitado seguir alimentándose de más personas”, lamentó Alejandra Guillén.

Recordó el caso de Teuchitlán, municipio de Jalisco, pues hizo visible el reclutamiento forzado y los circuitos de lugares donde retienen a las personas y que familias …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Ley de tierras: la calle dijo basta y frenó al Gobierno con su intento de más extranjerización
content:
Por Nahuel Lag


“La tierra no se vende, no se quema ni se desaloja”, dice una bandera, también una pancarta y lo grita alguien que pasa caminando. El que “no se vende” fue una victoria de la presión popular contra la “Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada”, cuando el Gobierno cedió el miércoles y quitó el capítulo de cuasi derogación de la Ley de Tierras. Pero a las 14 horas, cuando la Cámara de Senadores comenzó la sesión para tratar los otros capítulos de la normativa, miles de personas marchan al Congreso por Avenida de Mayo y desde las calles laterales de la Plaza Congreso exigiendo todavía que la tierra tampoco “se quema ni se desaloja”.


La masiva movilización que enfrentó a la lluvia y la represión de las fuerzas federales logró también, en la madrugada, que se quite el capítulo que modificaba la Ley de Manejo del Fuego. Así, el proyecto negociado con la UCR, PRO y bloques provinciales, sin apoyo social, obtuvo media sanción y mantiene otros dos capítulos críticos: la restricción a las expropiaciones y los desalojos exprés en tierras urbanas y rurales.


"Lo que hizo cambiar todo fue la presión popular"


La sesión empezó con una declaración de principios de La Libertad Avanza. El senador

Joaquín Benegas Lynch

, denunciado por tener una empresa que vende tierras a extranjeros, usó su “cuestión de privilegio” antes de iniciar el debate. En los bares sobre Avenida de Mayo se ve lo ve por televisión desde la calle. Lo que se escucha mientras son bombos y trompetas de la convocatoria hecha por las dos CTA, la UTEP y la CGT. También hay banderas del Frente de Sindicatos Unidos, muchas partidarias del peronismo y la izquierda; y más cerca del Congreso se ve a la Unión de Trabajadores y Trabajadoras de la Tierra (UTT), que ya realizó un nuevo verdurazo.


Foto: Plaga Colectiva


Ezequiel llegó desde Avellaneda y tiró la manta sobre Avenida de Mayo para vender el pañuelo de ocasión: “¡No a la Ley de Extranjerización!”, dice.


—¿Se vende el pañuelo de la patria no se vende?


—Sí, sale.


—¿A vos qué te parece el proyecto?


—No sé qué decirte. No estoy al tanto, estoy preocupado por tener para comer. Es difícil llegar a fin de mes y eso que no tengo hijos.


Miles de personas se ven más adelante, al costado del escenario montado por las organizaciones políticas, sindicales y sociales, el camión de la UTT, que llegó del cordón hortícola de La Plata para repartir alimentos entre la gente, eso que le falta a Ezequiel. Las organizaciones campesinas, junto a la Multisectorial por la Tierra y la Vivienda, denunciaron la gravedad del proyecto cuando sólo un grupo de organizaciones se manifestaba frente al Congreso en los otros cuatro intentos frustrados por aprobar la extranjerización de la tierra, desde el dictamen del 20 de mayo pasado.


“Lo que hizo cambiar todo fue la presión popular. Había un núcleo que veníamos impulsando el rechazo y después, obviamente, la Scaloneta en el partido contra Inglaterra y la bandera de ‘las Malvinas son Argentinas’ despertó el sentimiento de soberanía. Pudimos desenmascarar al gobierno ante la situación expresa de que toda la tierra y, sobre todo los recursos naturales, podían quedar en manos de los capitales extranjeros. Eso hizo que los gobernadores tengan que retirar el voto de sus senadores”, analiza Nahuel Levaggi, de la UTT y Mesa Agroalimentaria Argentina (MAA).


Las banderas con la tipografía de la bandera que usaron los jugadores de la Selección Argentina flotó en el aire por todos lados. El grito de fondo, insistía: “La patria no se vende”.


Ana es activista ambiental y llegó desde La Plata, tiene el texto escrito en un cartel con la bandera Argentina y en un pin en su campera. “Necesitamos defender lo que es nuestro. La tierra pertenece a quien la trabaja y a nuestros ancestros. No podemos permitir que vendan nuestra soberanía”.


Foto: Plaga Colectiva


La tierra no se vende


La derrota del capítulo de tierras se completó a 24 horas antes de la marcha, en una reunión de la presidente del bloque de La Libertad Avanza, Patricia Bullrich, con los aliados de la UCR, PRO y los legisladores que responden a los gobernadores Hugo Passalacqua (Misiones), Osvaldo Jaldo (Tucumán), Rolando Figueroa (Neuquén) y Gustavo Sáenz (Salta). Ellos fueron los que bajaron el pulgar. Bullrich, un día antes, había asegurado que tenía los votos en una conferencia de prensa con los presidentes de las comisiones de Asuntos Constitucionales, Agustín Coto (LLA), y de Legislación General …

author: anred
title: El Senado dio media sanción a la ley de Milei, pero la movilización anticipa una nueva batalla en Diputados
content:
Foto: collage con imágenes de Pilar Camacho (LN), Perfil y David Briasco (@registroovisual).


Tras más de cinco horas de represión de las fuerzas federales contra la multitudinaria movilización frente al Congreso, el Senado otorgó esta madrugada media sanción a lo que quedó del proyecto de Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada impulsado por el gobierno de Javier Milei. Con una diferencia de apenas cuatro votos, la iniciativa fue aprobada por 37 votos afirmativos contra 33 negativos, tras la derrota política del Gobierno, que se vio obligado a retirar, ante la fuerte presión social y la falta de apoyos parlamentarios, los capítulos que buscaban habilitar una profunda desregulación para la compra de tierras por parte de extranjeros y modificar la Ley de Manejo del Fuego. Aunque el Gobierno logró salvar el resto del proyecto, organizaciones ambientales, campesinas, indígenas, sindicales, políticas, sociales, culturales y de derechos humanos advirtieron que la norma mantiene artículos que habilitan desalojos exprés, restringen las expropiaciones y fortalecen un modelo de concentración de la tierra y de expansión extractivista. Tras la votación, la próxima disputa en las calles será impedir su aprobación definitiva en la Cámara de Diputados.

 Por ANRed.


Con

37 votos afirmativos, 33 negativos y dos ausencias

, el Senado otorgó esta madrugada media sanción al proyecto de Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada impulsado por el gobierno de Javier Milei. El oficialismo reunió los

20 votos propios de La Libertad Avanza

 y consiguió el respaldo de legisladores de la

UCR, el PRO y distintos bloques provinciales

, mientras que el rechazo estuvo integrado por el interbloque peronista, fuerzas provinciales y algunos sectores dialoguistas que finalmente no acompañaron la iniciativa. Estuvieron ausentes la senadora

Anabel Fernández Sagasti (PJ)

 y el senador

Flavio Fama (UCR)

.


Foto: Perfil.


Foto: Pilar Camacho (LN)


El resultado llegó luego de

uno de los mayores retrocesos legislativos sufridos por el Gobierno desde el inicio de su mandato

: ante el fuerte rechazo social, la creciente dificultad para reunir votos y una amplia campaña impulsada por organizaciones ambientales, campesinas, indígenas, sociales, políticas, culturales, sindicales y de derechos humanos,

el oficialismo se vio obligado a retirar el capítulo que modificaba la Ley de Tierras

 y que eliminaba prácticamente todas las restricciones para la adquisición de tierras rurales por parte de capitales extranjeros.

 También, el gobierno tuvo que resignar los

cambios en la Ley de Manejo del Fuego

, que buscaban

favorecer la compra de tierras y la habilitación de negocios inmobiliarios en tierras que sufren incendios forestales (por cuestiones naturales o por la acción humana deliberada)

.


La presión popular hizo retroceder al Gobierno y hoy se moviliza por la caída de toda la ley


CIUDAD DE BUENOS AIRES, ARGENTINA – 6 DE AGOSTO: Columnas de organizaciones sociales, agrupaciones agrarias y movimientos sindicales colman la Plaza del Congreso en rechazo al proyecto de ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada. La movilización multisectorial generó cortes totales de tránsito en las avenidas Callao y Entre Ríos durante la jornada. (Foto: David Briasco)


Así, el Gobierno sufrió un

duro revés

, no sólo en el debate parlamentario, sino también en

su capacidad para fijar el relato en la agenda de discusión y de

 

conversación pública

, al verse doblegado por

una fuerte resistencia social en las calles combinada con la aparición masiva de figuras artísticas por fuera de la política tradicional que se sumaron a la causa, dándole mayor alcance y repercusión.

Un hecho que también puede leerse como una

continuidad del debate público que se instaló por la soberanía nacional luego de que los jugadores de la Selección agitaran un trapo señalando que «Las Malvinas son argentinas» luego de haber vencido al seleccionado inglés en la última Copa del Mundo.

author: A.N.A.
title: [Espanha] Chamamento: Rumo a um Coletivo Silvestre e Comunal. Projeto
content:
Olá. Este é um chamamento.


Um sinal de fumaça.


“

Comunalizar,


não poderia ser de outra forma.


Reensilvestrar, ensilvestrar-se.

“


Queremos convocar pessoas que se sentem impulsionadas pela visão de contribuir para um mundo mais silvestre e comunal.


Em concreto, gostaríamos de promover a criação de um coletivo de convivência, uma comunidade de pessoas que cuidam de seu entorno natural com uma abordagem silvestre para suprir suas necessidades, reconstruindo as culturas comunitárias dentro de seu grupo e em seu território mais amplo.


Por “silvestre” entendemos uma forma de vida e de nos relacionarmos que busca voltar a fazer parte dos lugares que habitamos, diminuindo a dependência de estruturas estatais e industriais e recuperando e integrando práticas como a coleta de plantas e frutos, a caça, a pesca, ou o uso de materiais naturais para resolver as necessidades vitais. Vemos essas atividades não apenas como técnicas para suprir necessidades, mas como portas de entrada para outras formas de organização social, de autonomia e de relação com o território.


Para isso, consideramos imprescindível ocupar-se da regeneração dos processos naturais, do cuidado e do respeito ao entorno. Também propomos a convivência do silvestre com práticas agrícolas, pecuárias, florestais, etc., embora com a intenção de que ocupe um lugar central. Cientes das dificuldades atuais, queremos caminhar com firmeza nessa direção, sem julgamentos nem purismos, aproveitando as brechas e assumindo o caráter exploratório da tarefa.


Nessa mesma busca, gostaríamos de colocar no centro a recuperação de culturas e formas de organização comunitárias, que estiveram presentes na Península Ibérica desde tempos pré-históricos, nas quais a vizinhança cuida e usufrui do entorno que habita de maneira comum. Defender e promover os bens comuns, a autogestão, a democracia direta da assembleia aberta e os trabalhos coletivos, o pensar-se em comum entre vizinhos e vizinhas e com o território. Também nos referimos aos comuns mais modernos e aos diferentes movimentos e estruturas associativas nascidas em torno do comum. Há diversas maneiras de materializar tudo isso; em qualquer caso, nos parece que implica trabalhar tanto internamente no coletivo como com diferentes atores locais, vizinhos e vizinhas, bem como organizar-se com outros grupos afins.


Por fim, nessa visão cabem múltiplas formas de concretizar um coletivo de convivência, desde a vizinhança até uma economia comum, assim como diferentes abordagens de coletivizar os cuidados. Seja qual for, nos parece imprescindível atender ao processo interno do grupo de maneira consciente e ativa, cuidando do desenvolvimento pessoal e ocupando-se da estrutura e das dinâmicas grupais do coletivo.


Para nós, situar-se em uma vida mais silvestre e comunal é uma das maneiras de responder à crise ecossocial. Reconhecemos que há muitas maneiras, muitos lugares a partir dos quais repensar, agir e viver esse sistema. Neste momento e circunstâncias, tentamos contribuir a partir desta proposta, partindo de um legado que perdura desde as sociedades pré-estatais, e que hoje muitos movimentos estão recuperando e atualizando.


Em que ponto estamos


Esta proposta encontra-se em uma fase inicial. Nós, duas pessoas, a promovemos, desenvolvendo essa visão no meio rural e com a inquietação de gerar encontro e comunidade:


Gostaríamos de reunir pessoas interessadas em fazer parte da criação de um coletivo de convivência que coloque os eixos silvestre e comunal no centro. Por enquanto, não foi concretizado além da visão aqui descrita. A ideia é que o próprio grupo construa sua forma de vida, organização e localização, de acordo com suas necessidades, capacidades e desejos.


Também queremos conectar com pessoas que, embora não estejam pensando agora em fazer parte de uma comunidade de convivência, ressoem com essa visão e queiram explorar como impulsionar uma cultura mais silvestre e comunal em seus territórios.


Se isso te motiva, te interessa, gostaríamos de nos encontrar, convidar você a se aproximar e fazer parte do processo. A ideia é se conhecer, reunir-se em diferentes espaços de exploração, sondar o que se move e em quais direções.


Você pode nos escrever ou ligar contando quem é, de onde escreve, qual seu interesse e sua disponibilidade para participar de encontros.


Até breve!


Raquel e Gonzalo

silycom.valle@proton.me

author: Rizomatica
title: Se realizó Nutram por la defensa del Alerce costero en Ainil Leufu Valdivia
content:
El pasado 30 de julio nos reunimos en la Casa de la Memoria de Valdivia, en un Nütram por la defensa del Parque Nacional Alerce Costero. Junto a organizaciones, comunidades e individualidades de distintos territorios.


Este espacio nos permitió compartir conocimientos, dialogar y fortalecer la articulación frente al proyecto de construcción del segundo tramo de la carretera T720. Una iniciativa que amenaza la biodiversidad, los bosques nativos y las cuencas que protege este parque.


Agradecemos a todas las personas que participaron y contribuyeron a este encuentro, reafirmando que la defensa del territorio sólo es posible a través de la organización y el trabajo colectivo.


El Parque Nacional Alerce Costero no sólo resguarda un invaluable patrimonio natural, sino también un territorio ancestral del Pueblo Mapuche, cuya memoria y vínculo con este espacio permanecen vivos hasta hoy.


Defender este territorio es también defender el itxofil mongen, la memoria ancestral y el derecho de las futuras generaciones a heredar un territorio íntegro.


Exponentes:


Machi Cristóbal Tremihual futa Willimapu


Daniela Arriaza de Colectivo Raíces de Corral


Magdalena Contreras Voces del territorio


Dr. Antonio Lara de Corporación Alerce


Ejes Principales del Nütram:

Defensa del Territorio: Oposición al tramo 2 de la ruta vial T-720 por el daño irreversible a la biodiversidad costera.

Protección del Lahual: Resguardo del alerce (Fitzroya cupressoides), incluyendo el «Alerce Milenario» o «Abuelo» el árbol más antiguo del planeta.

Gobernanza Territorial: Compartir saberes ancestrales y científicos. Coordinar acciones entre comunidades de Valdivia, Corral y La Unión. 


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

author: Dyepeson Martins
title: Senado dos EUA aprova Daniel Perez antes de aval do Brasil para vaga de embaixador
content:
Em meio a tensões diplomáticas acentuadas nos últimos meses pelas ações dos Estados Unidos (EUA) na América Latina, o Senado norte-americano votou e aprovou, nesta sexta-feira (7), a indicação de Donald Trump à embaixada estadunidense no Brasil. Os senadores aprovaram o nome do representante da Flórida Daniel Perez. O parlamentar, no entanto, ainda precisa da

autorização do governo brasileiro

 para ocupar o cargo, como preconiza a Convenção de Viena, de 1961.


A votação teve início por volta das 14h20 (horário de Brasília) e ocorreu em bloco – processo mais rápido que inclui todas as indicações num só pacote. Além de Perez, outras 73 indicações de Donald Trump foram aprovadas em votação apertada, de 51 contra 47 rejeições – o Senado norte-americano tem 53 cadeiras republicanas.


Antes da votação, os senadores debateram sobre políticas educacionais e sanções ao governo de Vladimir Putin, na Rússia, numa sessão apressada, uma vez que a Casa entrará num recesso de cinco semanas e foi preciso negociar exatamente o que entraria na pauta e seria resolvido antes do retorno dos parlamentares, em setembro.


Perez tem 39 anos, é “anticomunista” e fiel à agenda do movimento nacionalista Make America Great Again (MAGA). Nos últimos dias, Trump reforçou a pressão ao Brasil pela aprovação do deputado, indicado em 1º de junho sem consulta prévia ao Itamaraty – protocolo também estabelecido pelas regras da diplomacia. Entre reações aos quase 70 dias à espera pelo aval brasileiro, os EUA revogaram o visto da embaixadora brasileira em Washington, Maria Luiza Viotti.


A

Agência Pública


mostrou

 que nomes poderosos influenciam a indicação de Perez para o cargo no Brasil: a chefe de gabinete da Casa Branca, Susie Wiles, e o secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio. Susie teria recompensado o parlamentar da Flórida pela oposição ferrenha a um inimigo político em comum: o governador Ron DeSantis. Já Rubio é amigo próximo de Perez e o teria como integrante de um projeto para combater o que ele classifica, sem provas, como “terrorismo de extrema esquerda” em outros países.


A insistência de Trump para que Perez assuma o cargo, vago desde janeiro de 2025 após a saída de Elizabeth Bagley, que esteve na função durante o governo Biden, ocorre num período estratégico: as eleições de 2026. A

Pública

 apontou como os EUA já vêm moldando o discurso para questionar o resultado das urnas eletrônicas em caso de derrota do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), na corrida à Presidência da República.


O bolsonarismo é a ala representativa da ultradireita no Brasil e aliada aos principais interesses ideológicos e econômicos da política trumpista, como a exploração de terras raras, a não regulamentação de Big Techs e a expansão da venda do biocombustível produzido em solo norte-americano.


Relação estremecida com o Brasil


Diante das ações de Trump, o presidente Lula subiu o tom e chamou de “irresponsável” e “impensada” a revogação do visto da embaixadora brasileira.


O impasse sobre a embaixada americana no Brasil ocorre num contexto de escalada da tensão entre os dois países desde o início do mandato de Donald Trump, em janeiro de 2025.


Entre as questões de maior conflito, está a recente aplicação das tarifas de 25% dos EUA à indústria brasileira. As taxas passaram a valer em 22 de julho e foram anunciadas seis dias antes pelo secretário de Estado, Marco Rubio, no X (antigo Twitter).


O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Mauro Vieira, classificou as medidas como “sem justificativa e lastro de realidade” e ainda acusou Donald Trump de tentar interferir no judiciário do Brasil após a carta enviada pelo presidente americano a Lula, em julho de 2025, para ameaçar novas tarifas.

author: Administrador
title: Inauguración «Encuentro de Artes y Encuentro de Resistencias y Rebeldías». 1 de agosto, 17:00 horas, Caracol de Morelia.
content:
Sábado 1 de agosto, 17:00 horas

Encuentro de Artes y Encuentro de Resistencias y Rebeldías

INMEDIATAMENTE DESPUÉS… GRAN BAILE POPULAR

Compañeras, companñeros, compañeres. Saludos solidarios. Deseo para ustedes y para todas las resistencias, que cobija la Madre Tierra en sus múltiples expresiones y geografías, que este encuentro y este tiempo permita fortalecer: la solidaridad en todas las necesidades, la pertenencia en la diversidad,  la articulación en la distancia y la organización en las diferencias. Que el corazón del cielo y el corazón de la tierra les siga guiando en esta digna lucha. Sinceramente, Elías García Comentario de Elías Iván García — agosto  2, 2026 @ 2:31 pm

author: CMI Argentina
title: Media sanción al proyecto de “propiedad privada” pero sin los cambios en la Ley de Manejo del Fuego
content:
El gobierno logró la media sanción del proyecto de Ley de “inviolabilidad de la propiedad privada” pero debió retirar también los cambios a la Ley de Manejo del Fuego. Fue cerca de la 1 y media de la mañana por 37 votos a favor y 33 del en contra, luego de una sesión de casi 12 horas que se realizó en medio de la represión a la marcha pacífica que se realizó frente al Congreso.


El oficialismo ya había tenido que dejar atrás el capitulo que facilitaba la acumulación de tierras en manos extranjeras, y antes de la votación también retiró el que eliminaba los límites a la venta y cambio de uso de tierras incendiadas en zonas de bosque nativo y áreas protegidas. Sí se aprobaron las limitaciones a las expropiaciones que puede hacer el Estado y la agilización de desalojos.


La senadora neuquina de

La Libertad Avanza Nadia Márquez

, reconoció que uno de los objetivos es poder desalojar por ejemplo a comunidades mapuches en su provincia:

 “Una señora a quien no conozco se llama

María Boers

, argentina, no es Mary, es María, es argentina, no es extranjera, adquirió alrededor de 600 hectáreas cerca de

Villa Langostura

. Llamativamente en el año 2012, 2011 perdón, le usurpan parte de su territorio, parte de sus hectáreas, grupos autodenominados mapuches. Ya hace 15 años que esta mujer


de casi 70 años, hace 15 años que no puede tener su propiedad privada”.


Con respecto a los límites que se ponen a las expropiaciones que puede hacer el estado el senador de

Unión por la Patria Mariano Recalde,

se busca que no se puedan recuperar las tierras y empresas que este gobierno venda:

“La modificación de la ley de expropiaciones lo que busca es hacer más caro, más dificultoso, más engorroso y judicializar todos los procesos de recuperación de las tierras y las empresas que este gobierno venda”.


Además,

Recalde

 criticó que se habilite también los desalojos en pocos días de inquilinos que se atrasen en el alquiler:

“Esta es la novedad de la modificación del régimen de desalojos. Incluir en los desalojos exprés al inquilino que tiene un contrato y se atrasa. En un contexto donde la gente no llega a fin de mes, en un contexto donde la gente es en deuda, en un contexto donde lo único que le preocupan es desalojarlo rápido cuando se atrasan un poco”


El proyecto con media sanción pasa ahora a la

 Cámara de Diputados.

title: Free but out of reach? The long wait for public mental health services
content:
Jem Curtny Narboneta, a BS psychology student, participates in the poster-making contest during Psychology Week celebration. Photo courtesy of Jem Curtny Narboneta.

“The biological aspect includes medicines and genetics,” Del Valle said. “But psychosocial factors—the social determinants of health—also affect us. If we improve education, if people have jobs, and communities can support them, these all contribute to mental health.”

Trigger warning: Mentions of suicide

By Kasheena Camacho Bulatlat.com

MANILA —  For Filipinos experiencing mental health crises, long waiting periods for free mental health consultations continue to hinder their access to care, forcing some of them to seek costly private treatment.

For March Lavela, 24, deciding to seek professional help came after months of grief, mounting family responsibilities, and worsening panic attacks. “The turning point for me was when the pressure built up so much that my body couldn’t handle it anymore,” Lavela said.

He said the panic attacks began during online thesis classes, where repeated confrontations with a professor became overwhelming. The anxiety persisted even outside the classroom, with merely hearing the professor’s name triggering panic.

“I knew it was time to ask for help when I started thinking about death and killing myself,” he said. “…[R]ealizing my mind was going to that dark place made me see that I couldn’t fight this on my own anymore.”

Unable to afford private psychiatric consultations, Lavela sought free mental health services. He booked consultations with both the Philippine General Hospital (PGH) and the National Center for Mental Health (NCMH). The available schedules, however, were months away.

“I decided to just walk in at NCMH because I knew I couldn’t wait for a far-off online appointment date,” he said. “I felt like if I waited that long, I might already be gone.”

At the NCMH, he disclosed to hospital personnel that he had been experiencing suicidal thoughts. “They assisted me through the whole process once I walked into the hospital,” he said.

Lavela’s experience mirrors a broader challenge confronting the country’s mental healthcare system.

Jem Curtny B. Narboneta, 21, also agonized over the waiting period to access care.

Narboneta, a psychology student, said she initially spent around P11,000 ($181) on several online psychological consultation platforms in search of answers.

She also contacted around 15 to 20 emergency hotlines she found online but said none responded.

Her mother later accompanied her to NCMH for free consultation. Instead of receiving immediate care, they were advised to secure an online appointment. Narboneta said the earliest available schedule was nearly a year away.

“Obviously I couldn’t wait that long because I’d be long gone if I were to wait a year,” she said.

Unable to wait, she then sought consultation with a private psychiatric facility despite the additional cost.

“It greatly affected my well-being because I needed mental health consultation that time,” she said. “To find out I had to wait a year made me think of all the people who finally mustered the courage to seek help only to discover mental health services weren’t as accessible as they thought.”

Lavela and Narboneta are among the thousands of Filipinos seeking professional mental health services in the past years.

In an online interview with Bulatlat , Dr. Teresa Rosalie D. del Valle, a medical specialist IV at the NCMH, said that consultations have increased significantly in recent years.

“The pandemic heightened public awareness of mental health,” Del Valle said.

The increase in demand, however, has outpaced the country’s available mental health workforce, according to both Del Valle and international data.

According to the World Health Organization’s Mental Health Atlas 2024 , the Philippines has only 3.9 mental health workers for every 100,000 population, including 0.2 psychiatrists, 0.3 psychologists, 0.7 mental health nurses, 1.1 social workers, and 1.6 other mental health workers per 100,000 population.

The report also recorded one specialized mental hospital, 22 psychiatric units in general hospitals, and 1,362 community-based outpatient mental health facilities nationwide.

Del Valle said the current number of psychiatrists remains insufficient to keep up with the growing number of patients seeking care.

title: ‘Not Fair NEET, But Ban NEET’: Hunger Strike Against NEET Enters Seventh Day in Chennai
content:
The indefinite hunger strike against the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) in Chennai entered its seventh day on Saturday, August 8. The agitation, led by the Anti-NEET Federation and the Joint Movement Against NEET, is demanding not merely reforms to the examination but its complete abolition, along with greater state control over education.


 


Chennai, August 8, 2026:

 An indefinite hunger strike demanding the abolition of the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) entered its seventh day in Chennai on Saturday, with four anti-NEET activists continuing their fast at Koyambedu.


 


The four hunger strikers —

Dhanasekar, Jeeva, Puliyanthope Mohan and Ravi

 — are associated with the Ban NEET Movement of the Anti-NEET Federation in Tamil Nadu. The Joint Movement Against NEET is demanding the abolition of NEET, greater state autonomy over education and a designated public space in Chennai where the protesters can continue their agitation peacefully. One of the four hunger-strikers, Ravi was hospitalised on Thursday after coughing up blood. His condition is now reported to be stable.


 


The protesters are demanding that the TVK-led Tamil Nadu government pass a fresh Assembly resolution or Bill seeking exemption from NEET and pursue the pending legal challenge concerning the state’s earlier attempt to secure an exemption. They have also called for the government to provide a permanent public venue for peaceful protests in Chennai.


 


“We will call off the hunger strike if a resolution is passed. That’s the first step. Then, we need an alternative location to carry on with our protest against the exam,” said

S Manirathinam

, brother of S Anitha, whose death in 2017 became a defining moment in Tamil Nadu’s opposition to NEET.


 


Manirathinam urged the Tamil Nadu government to reaffirm its opposition to NEET through a fresh Assembly resolution or Bill. He said previous AIADMK and DMK governments had passed resolutions and a Bill seeking an exemption and argued that a renewed initiative would demonstrate that opposition to NEET cuts across party lines.


 


He also called for the state government to expedite its legal challenge to the President’s decision to withhold assent to the earlier exemption Bill passed in the state assembly.


 


‘Not fair NEET, but ban NEET’


 


The Anti-NEET Federation, a collective of students’ and youth organisations and social workers, says its demand goes beyond seeking reforms that will make NEET more transparent or prevent examination malpractice.


 


Its position is unequivocal:

NEET itself should be abolished

.


 


The federation argues that NEET favours students who can afford expensive private coaching and additional years of preparation, placing students from rural, government-school and marginalised communities at a great disadvantage. The Joint Movement Against NEET has similarly argued that the examination has deepened inequalities in access to medical education and contributed to the expansion of the private coaching industry. Its press statement also cited nearly 40 student deaths in Tamil Nadu, including those of Anitha, Pratheeba and Anukreethika, which it linked to examination pressure, systemic inequalities and unequal access to opportunities.


 


The federation is also demanding that states be allowed greater freedom to determine medical admissions, including the use of Plus Two examination marks, and that education be moved from the Concurrent List back to the State List.


 


Dhanasekar said the hunger strike began after the protesters were denied permission to hold a peaceful public demonstration, despite an assurance reportedly given during earlier anti-NEET protests.


 


School Education Minister A Rajmohan visited the protest site on Wednesday, reiterated the government’s opposition to NEET and appealed to the protesters to withdraw their fast, Dhanasekar said. “We will end the hunger strike only if the government allots us a public place to continue our agitation peacefully,” he said.


 


Anitha’s name remains at the heart of the anti-NEET struggle


 


Do you remember S Anitha?


 


During the month-long protests against NEET at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, her name was repeatedly invoked by protesters from Tamil Nadu. For the anti-NEET movement, her memory is not merely commemorative. It is political.


 


Anitha was a

Dalit student

from Ariyalur district and the daughter of an

 agricultural daily-wage labourer …

author: rti_admin
title: Does Ambedkar Posthumously Have a ‘Homeland’?
content:
In August 1931, during his first formal meeting with Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi at Mani Bhavan in Bombay, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar made a declaration that fundamentally shattered the nationalist illusion of a unified anti-colonial front: “Gandhiji, I have no homeland.” To grasp the profound weight of this statement, one must first interrogate what it truly means to call a place a “homeland.” A homeland is not merely a geographic expanse bounded by political borders, nor is it defined simply by possessing a passport or a constitutional territory. A homeland is a space of radical belonging—a site where an individual can exist freely, with uncompromised dignity and fundamental liberty. In his autobiography, Nelson Mandela captured this primal essence of freedom when he wrote: “I was not born with a hunger to be free. I was born free—free in every way that I could know. Free to run in the fields near my mother’s hut, free to swim in the clear stream that ran through my village, free to roast mealies under the stars and ride the broad backs of slow-moving bulls.” For Mandela, as for any human being, a true homeland is a place where freedom is the natural baseline of existence.

At a time when anti-colonial dissent was at its peak, Ambedkar’s blunt denial of the undisputed leader of the independence struggle was an act of extreme political honesty. It laid bare his genuine sense of alienation on behalf of his people. How could a man claim a homeland in a nation that systematically denied his basic human dignity? For the Untouchables, the daily tyranny of caste Hindu society—expressed through forced segregation, denial of public water, physical violence, and systemic humiliation—was far more immediate, brutal, and historically entrenched than British colonial rule. Ambedkar recognized that while Gandhi fought against British colonialism, the upper-caste leadership was eager to preserve its internal feudal empire. To declare to Gandhi that a country built on social injustice is a prison for its most oppressed people, not a homeland, was an act of profound refusal.

Today, as youth-led demonstrations at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar—organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over widespread NEET paper leaks and national examination irregularities—draw thousands of marchers, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and his companions carry “a photo of Dr. Bhim Rao Ambedkar, M.K. Gandhi, and a copy of the Indian Constitution” to ensure their protests remain peaceful. As mainstream civil society, student unions, and GenZ youth movements routinely frame Gandhi and Ambedkar side-by-side as twin patrons of democratic dissent, an urgent Ambedkarite critique demands to be posed: Has post-colonial India posthumously constructed a “home” for Ambedkar by diluting his radical anti-caste framework into a sanitized, state-sanctioned icon, paired with the very ideology he spent his life dismantling?

It is widely assumed today that Ambedkar eventually found his “home” in the post-colonial Indian Republic. The dominant narrative holds that the drafting of the Constitution, the formal abolition of untouchability under Article 17, and his elevation to national icon status granted him and his people the homeland he was denied in 1931. However, we must critically interrogate the difference between the “home” Ambedkar spoke of then and the “home” offered to his people now. The homeland Ambedkar envisioned was not merely a territorial entity with a flag and a legal code. It was a true social democracy anchored in pratitya-samutpada (interconnectedness), liberty, equality, and fraternity. It was a home where the annihilation of caste restored moral community, dignity, and real political agency to the depressed classes. What the post-colonial Indian state offers instead is a structural illusion: a constitutional home on paper, accompanied by an unchanged Brahminical social order in practice. The state eagerly claims Ambedkar as the “Father of the Constitution” to validate its democratic credentials globally, yet actively strips his memory of its radical, anti-caste methodology.

To claim that Ambedkar or Dalits have found a home in modern India is to ignore their daily lived reality deliberately. Are Dalits no longer facing discrimination? The empirical reality tells a devastating story. The “home” constructed by the modern nation-state remains a site of ongoing, systemic violence for Dalits. Untouchability has not vanished; it has merely adapted to modernity. When a Dalit …

author: Benjamin Cordero
title: Ang Paglalayag sa Kawalan: Isang Pagsusuri sa The Odyssey (2026)
content:
Isang dambuhalang tagumpay sa sining ng pelikula ang The Odyssey (2026) ni Christopher Nolan. Bagaman napakamahal na ng halaga ng sine sa kasalukuyang panahon, isa itong biswal na hiyas na nararapat panoorin sa pinakamalaking telon hangga’t maaari. Ngunit sa ilalim ng nagngangalit na alon ng Dagat Mediteranyo o sa sindak na dulot ng Cyclops o sa bigat ng modernong pagganap na dala ni Matt Damon, may kuwentong pumipintig sa isang napakapamilyar na paraan.

Ang panonood ng The Odyssey sa pamamagitan ng matang Pilipino ay parang nakararanas ng matinding déjà vu . Para sa isang kulturang hinubog ng pangingibang-bansa, walang-katapusang pagtitiis, at pagkakawatak-watak ng pamilya, ang sampung taong pakikipagsapalaran ni Odysseus para lang makauwi ay hindi lang kuwento ng mitolohiyang Griyego—ito mismo ang buhay at kalagayan ng modernong Pilipino.

Ang pinakamabilis at pinakamatinding koneksyon ng pelikula ni Nolan sa buhay-Pilipino ay ang karakter mismo ni Odysseus. Siya ay isang lalaking nakakulong sa isang walang-awa at nakapapagod na pagpapatapon sa sarili. Sa pelikula, mariing ipinakita ni Nolan ang sikolohikal na epekto ng pagkakahiwalay ni Odysseus sa kanyang bayan; hindi lang siya lumalaban sa mga halimaw, kundi lumalaban din siya sa oras, sa distansya, at sa unti-unting paglaho ng alaala ng tahanang kanyang iniwan.

Ito ang salamin ng totoong buhay ng milyun-milyong Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), ang ating mga bagong bayani. Katulad ni Odysseus na umalis ng Ithaca para lumaban sa digmaan sa Troy para sa kanyang bayan, ang OFW ay umaalis din sa Pilipinas para lumaban sa isang digmaang pang-ekonomiko sa dayuhang lupain. Pareho silang ginagabayan ng iisang layunin: ang buhayin, protektahan, at sa huli ay balikan ang pamilyang kanilang minamahal.

Kapag nakatulala si Odysseus (Matt Damon) sa karagatan habang nakakulong sa isla ng Ogygia, sinumang Pilipinong nanonood ay makikita ang mukha ng ating mga tita, tito, ina, at ama na nagpupuyat habang nakatingin sa bintana ng mga matataas na gusali sa Hong Kong, Dubai, o Singapore. Ang mga halimaw na hinarap ni Odysseus—ang mapanlinlang na akit ni Circe o ang nakaparalisang pagkalimot na dala ng mga Lotus-Eater—ay madaling maitumbas sa mga panganib ng pangingibang-bansa ngayon: (1) Ang tuksong makiangkop nang tuluyan sa dayuhang kultura at limutin ang sariling pinagmulan. (2) Ang mabigat at mapag-isang depresyon ng pagiging dayuhan sa ibang bansa at; (3) Ang mga burukrasya, kahirapan sa bayang babalikan at pisikal na hadlang na nagpapatagal sa pag-uwi nang maraming taon, o dekada.

Habang nakikipaglaban si Odysseus sa malalaking alon, ang bigat ng emosyon ng pelikula ay pasan naman nina Penelope (Anne Hathaway) at Telemachus (Tom Holland) sa Ithaca. Mahusay na ipinakita ni Nolan na ang Ithaca ay hindi isang marangyang kaharian na naghihintay sa kanilang hari, kundi isang gumuguhong bahay na kinatatawanan ng mga mapagsamantalang manliligaw/dayuhan na unti-unting nagpapasasa sa kanilang yaman.

Ang bahaging ito ng kuwento ay napakasakit tanggapin para sa mga pamilyang Pilipino. Kapag ang isang magulang ay umalis ng Pilipinas para magtrabaho sa abroad, ang pamilyang naiwan ay parang nakabinbin sa hangin. Si Penelope ang sumasalamin sa nakatutunaw at mapag-isang dusa ng asawang naiwan—na kadalasan ay ang ina na mag-isang nagtataguyod sa bahay, nagpoprotekta sa mga anak laban sa mga mapagsamantalang tao sa lipunan, at nagkukunwaring matatag kahit na nadudurog ang puso sa tindi ng pangungulila.

Si Telemachus naman ang kumakatawan sa “anak ng OFW.” Ipinakita ni Tom Holland ang isang binatang puno ng kumplikadong emosyon—may galit, may pangungulila, at may matinding pressure. Lumaki siya sa ilalim ng anino ng isang tanyag na ama na halos hindi niya matandaan, at napilitang ipagtanggol ang kanilang tahanan bago pa siya maging handa. Sa pang-araw-araw na buhay ng Pilipino, ito ang realidad ng milyun-milyong bata na lumalaki sa pamamagitan lamang ng video calls at remittance slips. Lumalaki silang walang ama o ina sa tabi, napipilitang magmatured nang maaga, nakalantad sa nauusong karahasan (maging sa sariling paaralan) at pasan ang bigat ng sakripisyo ng magulang habang nahihirapan ding kilalanin ang sarili.

author: Kevin Lin
title: The Seven Deadly Sins of Conferencing
content:
Many of us know from experience that the most memorable and enjoyable parts of participating in a conference are the tea and coffee breaks, the conversations lunches and dinners, the informal chats outside of the conference room while the meeting is still happening, and the late-night hangouts with other participants. Genuinely good conversations take place and relationships are formed or renewed in those moments. So why don’t we recognise what is obvious, and create structures that bring out these experiences?


Social movements rely on purposeful gatherings to connect, share experiences, and strategise. We do this so often we should be really good at it. But more often than not, things do not seem to quite work. This has prompted me to reflect, and then test my impressions with other conference-goers who turn out to be feeling much the same ways. I need to first acknowledge how much unseen labour goes into any event planning; the event organisers are the most invisible if everything goes well. But it is necessary to recognise and name things that do not seem to work.


Here are the seven deadly sins of conference organising. I want to speak to my fellow conference organisers: of course, not all of us committed all of the sins, and some of you have done much better. But many of the sins would sound familiar to us, and we often let our guards down. By naming them, we may do a better job at avoiding them, and get to organise and experience more effective, creative and joyful gatherings.


 


Greed


 


The first sin is greed. We are often greedy about what can be accomplished with a gathering, especially with sizable conferences. We want to invite many people to be there to meet and connect, while also want them to have substantial discussions.


A medium to large conference of dozens to a few hundred people is amazing. But it is not primarily a place for deep learning or for substantial conversations despite our best efforts and most sincere wishes. There are simply too many sessions, too many speakers and too many people to learn and engage deeply. We listen to one panel after another and hardly remember anything from each speaker, while facilitators apologise for running out of time and no more time for questions. We then try to have conversations during breaks that on average last for 5 to 10 minutes before rushing back to the next session or talking or introducing ourselves to someone else. You should not feel alone in experiencing this.


We know deep learning and substantial conversation are most likely to take place in much smaller meetings. You may really have to keep it to a very small number of participants, arguably no more than 10 or 15 but maybe even fewer, to have sustained conversations that give everyone time to think, allow ideas to develop, and for them to build on each other’s ideas.


The medium and large conferences serve other important goals: it is good for building new relationships or renewing old ones, for feeling part of a larger movement with many others with shared values and goals, and for experiencing the optimism and joy of movement-building. It is good enough to take away with you the connections you have made, a sense of the movement’s diversity and creativity, and the fact that people are doing the best they can under enormous pressure and risk.


If these are the realistic goals, then our task is to structure the events in ways that let people and ideas to breath, to have both structured discussions and unstructured time for spontaneous conversations, and to make these events into festivals.


 


Busyness


 


The second sin is busyness. Far too often, I have been in conference planning where the logistics – the venue search and booking, the travel arrangement, the drinks, snacks and meals, and the interpretation – take up most of the planning time. We end up spending very little time discussing and experimenting with the actual program. In fact, the program design at times feels like an afterthought.


The logistics discussions and preparations are often not completely done until the very last minute. Time for a program discussion tends to be squeezed in between logistics discussions. When we are tight on time, we tend to revert to the familiar and the safest: let us get these speakers speakers for these panels, and each speaks for 15 minutes. It is the least that can go wrong. No one can claim they love this, but we keep doing it anyway.


It may be worth aiming to reserve a …

author: Rojava IC
title: Sleeper-Cell Report June 2026 – Justice Palace Department’s Head Killed
content:
The head of the Palace of Justice was seriously injured after being targeted in an attack on June 16. 


 


Key Points 


Five sleeper cell attacks were recorded in June; a slight increase from only three in May


A total of four military personnel were killed, and at least two injured 


Fatalities of two suspected ISIS affiliates were also recorded


Paper leaflets containing Pro-ISIS propaganda were distributed in several provinces throughout Syria


 


In Depth


This month, RIC recorded a total five attacks, two of which have been directly claimed by ISIS at the time of writing, the remaining three are believed to have been carried out by ISIS members.


On June 15, unidentified gunmen believed to be of an ISIS cell attacked the headquarters of general security forces, two of its members were killed and several others injured, west of Raqqa city, before one of the attackers self-detonated.  


On June 16, Salah Ahmad al-Saleh, head of the Palace of Justice in the town of Babila in rural Damascus was seriously injured by an explosive device attached to his vehicle. And on the same day, ISIS members targeted an oil tanker with machine-gun fire near the northern city of Manbij. Material damage to the tanker was reported.


On June 20, unidentified gunmen believed to be part of an ISIS cell, attacked members of the 76th Armored Division, causing the death of two Division’s members. The attack occurred near Tahnah junction in the western countryside of Manbij.


On June 24, two gunmen believed to be ISIS members, on a motorcycle opened fire on two members of the Engineering Regiment of the 72nd Division, on Ain Issa Road in Raqqa countryside, injuring both of them. 


On June 19, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces conducted an airstrike in northwest Syria. CENTCOM confirmed the killing of Ali Husayn al-‘Ulaywi, a senior ISIS leader. 


Paper leaflets were distributed in several mosques across different areas in Daraa, Idlib and Aleppo provinces. The leaflets contain extremist content and rhetoric linked to ISIS.


Save the Children, an Australian children’s advocacy organization, called for the return of an ISIS-linked Australian woman and her disabled child from Syria after a failed repatriation attempt. Following the failed departure, Syrian authorities reportedly transferred them to a detention facility in northwestern Syria’s Idlib Governorate, since then, her family lost contact with her.


Another Australian woman was accused of supporting ISIS and appeared before a court in Melbourne, where prosecutors alleged she lived in a household that held a teenage girl in slavery while the victim was subjected to repeated abuse.  Her request for bail was rejected, as prosecutors argued she poses a risk to public safety. 


Tammy Bruce, U.S. Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ambassador said that it would continue working with Syria to combat ISIS, and support efforts to preserve stability and safety in the country.

author: Unknown
title: Journalist Deniz Fırat remembered on the twelfth anniversary of her martyrdom
content:
Leyla Yıldıztan, who was born in 1984 in Xecîxatun village in Çaldıran district of Van province, was known as Deniz Fırat in the PKK ranks. Since her village was located on the border between Turkey and Iran, her family was repeatedly subject to attacks. For this reason, her family moved to Maku in 1990 and then to Urmia in Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan, Iran). After a while, they settled in Xakûrkê in southern Kurdistan (northern Iraq).


Deniz, who stayed in Xakûrkê in 1991-1992, witnessed the attacks on Southern Kurdistan with the co-operation of the Turkish state and the ruling party, KDP. In this process, Deniz and her sister Sarya (Sakine Yıldıztan), influenced by the martyrdom of Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş) who rejected the KDP's betrayal and chose resistance, decided to join the PKK. Her sister Binewş (Ayfer Yıldıztan), who had joined the PKK before Deniz, was martyred in a clash in Zap in 1997. Deniz only heard about the martyrdom of his sister Sarya, with whom she had joined the struggle, two years later, on 8 August 1999. Deniz was active in many areas in the guerrilla ranks and started to take part in press and media activities in 2007.


Starting her career in the press with the magazine "Tanrıça Zilan" [Zilan the Goddess], she also worked for the "Dengê Welat" [Voice of Homeland] radio. Later, in Maxmur Camp, she reported news for "Rojeva Welat" newspaper and various TV channels and agencies. She also wrote articles for the magazine "Zilan the Goddess". As a revolutionary journalist, she closely followed the attacks launched by ISIS against Maxmur on 6 August and lost her life on 8 August 2014.


On the twelfth anniversary of her martyrdom, Deniz Fırat was commemorated at her grave in the rural neighborhood of Xeçxatun in Van’s Çaldıran district.


In addition to her family, those attending the commemoration included representatives of the Mesopotamian Women Journalists Association (MKG), the Van branches of the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Association for Solidarity, Unity, Culture and Mutual Assistance with Families Who Lost Their Relatives in the Cradle of Civilizations (MEBYA-DER), members of the Peace Mothers Assembly, district executives of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), and numerous journalists.


Ceylan Şahinli, a member of the MKG Van branch, said: “Like those who followed in her footsteps, Deniz Fırat carried on the tradition she came from. At a time when the whole world feared ISIS, she fought with her camera. Just like those who paid the price in the struggle for truth, she too gave her life for this cause.”


Deniz Fırat’s brother, Seyat Yıldıztan, said: “Deniz is not only our martyr but also the martyr of her party and her people. She fought with her camera, not for herself or for her family, but for all her people.”


DEM Party Çaldıran District Co-Chair Abbas Aksak also spoke, saying: “When the Kurdish people were attacked by ISIS, Deniz worked with her camera and her pen, reporting on the attacks for the entire world to see. She continued her struggle until the day she was martyred on August 8. She is a martyr of Kurdistan and of the free press.”


The commemoration concluded with participants placing flowers on her grave.

author: James McVicar
title: Europe boils and burns: capitalism’s climate hellscape
content:
If you want to know how many lives our rulers are willing to sacrifice to defend the fossil fuel industry, you could start by looking at Europe. A heatwave that swept over huge swathes of the continent in June may have killed as many as

25,000 people

, according to one estimate from Indiana University. More than 3,000 in Spain and more still in Germany. The French national health agency has recorded

more than 5,700 excess deaths

. In many cities and towns, temperatures reached above 40 degrees Celsius.

Extreme heat is a major cause of weather-related death, if not

the

 major cause. It is a brutal way to die.

As the body desperately tries to offload heat by redirecting blood flow to the skin, the heart comes under increasing strain. Internal organs can start to disintegrate and leach toxins into the bloodstream. You can lose more than a litre of fluid every hour through sweat, which can cause a drop in blood pressure and lead to kidney failure.

Extreme heat also aggravates existing health conditions, which is why older people are particularly vulnerable. In France, about two-thirds of the excess deaths in June’s heatwave were people aged 75 and older.

The effects of extreme heat also intersect with the inequalities entrenched by capitalism. Women spend 30-50 percent more of their working day above heat stress thresholds, according to University of London researcher Laurie Parsons in an interview with DW, and they are

over-represented in heatwave deaths

. A 2021 study found that extreme urban heat exposure has

increased drastically since the 1980s

—mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and southern Asia.

Europe has been trapped under a heat dome: a mass of high-pressure air that traps heat like a lid and prevents clouds from forming. This in turn led to diabolical wildfires across France and Spain in July that forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee for safety. In such extreme weather conditions, wildfires can generate their own thunderstorms. The technical term is pyrocumulonimbus, but NASA calls them “fire-breathing dragon” clouds.

This is the hellish world capitalism is creating for more and more of us every day. It’s not just happening in Europe but all over the world. As a result of climate change, formerly extreme and rare weather events are becoming more frequent and more intense under the impacts of climate change. More heat domes, more mass deaths and raging infernos.

Analysis by a consortium of climate scientists from World Weather Attribution found that the June heatwave in Europe

would not have been possible

 without climate change. The pyrocumulonimbus cloud produced by the fires in France was the first one ever to be recorded in the country.

We know what’s behind all this: the continued extraction and burning of fossil fuels, driven by capitalism. The CSIRO states that about

90 percent

 of the world’s fossil fuel carbon emissions—the main cause of global temperature rises—comes from the burning of coal, oil and gas. In 2024, it was estimated that half of all planet-warming carbon dioxide emissions could be traced back to just

32 companies

, according to figures from the

CarbonMajors database

.

And cooking the globe is extremely good business. According to research by Oxfam, the six biggest fossil fuel companies doubled their profits for the second quarter of 2026, raking in

$46 billion

 compared to a measly $23 billion in the first three months of the year. They’re planning to increase their oil and gas production by 14 percent by 2030.

And this is not just a question of a handful of unregulated cowboy companies holding the rest of the world to ransom. CarbonMajors notes that in 1924,

17 of the top 20 carbon-emitting companies

 were state-owned, rather than private corporations. More to the point, fossil fuels are profitable only because of capitalism’s insatiable demand for them. Energy grids are built around them. Global shipping networks depend upon them. They’re a key ingredient in the production of plastics, fertilisers and construction materials. Militaries could not function without them.

The whole system of capitalism is defined by the competitive drive for profit. Capitalists control the world’s productive resources and will put those resources into motion only if they can turn a profit and secure a competitive advantage over their rivals. As long as this remains society’s motive force, the rich and powerful will go on burning fossil fuels to the very last drop …

author: Susan Price
title: Peru: Far-right Fujimori sworn in as president, amid protests
content:
Keiko Fujimori, leader of the far-right Popular Force party, was sworn in as Peru’s president on July 28, after narrowly defeating leftist candidate Roberto Sánchez in the run-off election in June.

Fujimori is the daughter of former dictator Alberto Fujimori, who imposed a United States-sponsored “shock therapy” in the 1990s, privatising public enterprises, eliminating state subsidies, further deregulating the economy and attacking labour laws.

Fujimori represents the continuation of her father’s policies and has maintained the neoliberal status quo through her party’s control of Congress since 2016 and other state institutions, such as the judiciary.

In her first address, Fujimori pledged to combat “insecurity” and has previously promised to fight crime with an “iron fist”. She said the military will take control during “states of emergency”, which have been used by successive right-wing governments to suspend freedom of assembly, movement and privacy.

The falsity of Fujimori’s supposed “anti-crime” agenda is laid bare by her and her party’s record of brazen corruption and facilitating organised crime. She was imprisoned in pre-trial detention for her role in the Odebrecht bribery scandal and for using illicit money to fund presidential campaigns. As president, she is now immune from prosecution.

Moreover, 15 of Fujimori’s 19 cabinet members have faced criminal investigations or been imprisoned for corruption, theft, fraud, embezzlement and assault. Vice President Luis Galarreta is currently under investigation for money laundering, abuse of authority and links to organised crime, while environment minister Vladimiro Huaroc has 51 investigations against him.

Fujimori’s supposed “tough-on-crime” approach also does not extend to the heinous crimes committed by the police and military when inflicting violence against Peru’s working class.

The Fujimorista-controlled Congress approved Law 32735 on July 21, which allows crimes committed by the police and military to be investigated and tried by police and military courts. Ongoing investigations and trials can now be transferred from civilian courts or stopped, including cases where police and military have already been convicted.

This adds to the widespread impunity already enjoyed by police and soldiers, who have killed at least 50 people in anti-government protests since 2022. Recently, a police officer shot and killed an eight-year-old boy in Huacho, a town about 150 kilometres north of Lima.

During her address, Fujimori lamented that Peru’s economic inequality is the highest in Latin America and pledged, in a populist move, to raise the minimum wage by 15%, to 1300 soles (A$545) a month. She knows this will have a negligible impact on big business bottom lines and workers’ living standards, in a country where more than 70% work in the informal economy, with no guaranteed minimum wage and basic work entitlements.

In many ways, Fujimori and her father are responsible for entrenching the neoliberal model that makes Peru one of the most unequal countries in the world. The top 1% control almost half (44.7%) of the country’s wealth, while the bottom 50% control just 0.1%.

Under this model, domestic and transnational corporations are granted almost free reign to pillage the country’s vast mineral deposits to make obscene profits.

Meanwhile, the concentration of the economy into monopolies and oligopolies — particularly in the agribusiness industry — results in price fixing and rising living costs. The basic family basket — the cost of basic goods and services for a family of four for a month — is more than 1860 soles ($779.29), which Fujimori’s promised wage raise covers less than 70% of.

Joining the far-right shift in governments in the region, Fujimori seeks to deepen ties with the United States and other far-right leaders in the region. Her inauguration was attended by far-right leaders, such as Chilean President José Antonio Kast and Argentine President Javier Milei.

She pledged to join US President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas, which aims to reassert US economic and military dominance in Latin America.

Thousands protested in the country’s capital, Lima, against Fujimori’s inauguration, rightly pointing out her role in introducing laws that facilitate crime and grant impunity to the military and police. Among the protesters were relatives of some of the thousands of people tortured, killed and disappeared under her father’s regime.

author: Sheree Lowe
title: Our Children are the Treaty generation
content:
This

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day

, we have an opportunity to reflect on something remarkable. 


Across Victoria, our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are growing up in one of the most significant political moments since colonisation. They are the first generation of children to grow up in

Victoria’s Treaty era

. Treaty is about far more than legal agreements or institutional reform. At its heart, Treaty is about people, and most importantly, our children, and our future generations. 


The true measure of any Treaty will not be found in the number of agreements reached or milestones achieved. It will be measured by whether it truly improves the lives of future generations. 


Will Aboriginal children grow up healthier? Will their identity and Connection to their Culture be strong? Will they have every opportunity to learn, thrive and lead? Will they inherit systems that recognise their strengths rather than focus on their disadvantage? 


These are the questions that really matter. 


Aboriginal children already possess extraordinary strengths. They inherit the oldest continuing culture on Earth. They are surrounded by families, Elders and Communities who pass on knowledge, stories and traditions – keeping them strong and keeping them connected to who they are. 


But despite their strengths, many Aboriginal children continue to experience inequitable outcomes across

health

, education,

incarceration

, and wellbeing. Too often, systems have been designed to exclude Aboriginal people and their families, rather than include them.  


Treaty is our chance to change this.  


Treaty allows us to shift decision-making closer to Aboriginal communities, strengthening self-determination and creating services that better reflect the aspirations, cultures and needs of Aboriginal children and families. 


This is not simply about changing policies. It is about changing possibilities. 


Imagine growing up as an Aboriginal child.

Imagine instead of growing up in a State that perpetuates stigma, stereotypes and wants to dismiss your culture in dark history books – you grow up knowing who you are, where you belong and actually understanding your Country and Culture.  


Children have the potential to grow up in a state where their Culture is not only respected but embedded throughout education, healthcare and public life.  Our collective history recognised, our languages celebrated and Community empowered to shape the services that support our families. 


Imagine knowing that decisions about your future are increasingly made by your own people, your Community.

That is the promise that Treaty represents. 


For today’s Aboriginal children, this is not some distant vision. It is unfolding right now, during their own childhood. 


They are the first generation who will remember Victoria before Treaty, and who will one day tell their own children what it was like to witness this historic transformation. 


That is both exciting and humbling, but it also places an extraordinary responsibility on all of us. 


Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day reminds us that children are not just our future leaders – they are citizens of today. Their experiences matter. Their ideas matter. Their voices matter. 


If Treaty is truly about creating a better future, then Aboriginal children must remain at the centre of every conversation. 


Because when today’s children become tomorrow’s Elders, they will not judge this generation by the complexity of negotiations or the wording of agreements. 


They will judge us by outcomes. 


Did we create a Victoria where Aboriginal children could grow up proud of who they are? Did we ensure they remained connected to Culture, Country and Community?  Did we reduce the inequities they inherited? Did we create opportunities for every Aboriginal child and their family to flourish and thrive? 


The answers to those questions will be the enduring measure of success. 


So, this Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day, let us recognise that our children are growing up during a defining chapter in our state’s history, and work together to ensure it’s done right.


We all must take pride in being the first Australian state to take this historic step and ensure that Treaty is not repealed after the state election. 


Because Treaty is a promise to our future generations.  


A promise that they are not simply growing up in the era of Treaty …

author: AWSM
title: A Kiwi Dies in Ukraine: The War Between Empires and the People Sent to Fight It
content:
Aotearoa Workers Solidarity Movement

The death of a New Zealand man, Samuel Haines,  fighting in Ukraine was reported in the familiar language used whenever ordinary people are consumed by war. He was described through his personal history, his motivations, his family and his decision to travel across the world to take part in a conflict that had nothing to do with the daily lives of most people in Aotearoa. What was not highlighted was the fact that the tragedy of war is that those who suffer most are usually not the people who create wars. Politicians, generals and corporate interests make decisions from offices far away from the front lines, while working-class people are asked to sacrifice their bodies in the name of nations they did not create and systems they do not control.

The death of a Kiwi volunteer in Ukraine raises questions that go beyond one individual. Why are people from countries on the other side of the world being drawn into a conflict between major powers? Why has a war involving Russia, Ukraine, NATO and competing geopolitical interests been presented to millions of people as a simple battle between good and evil? And what does the presence of far-right nationalist forces within Ukraine’s military tell us about the way states use ideology and violence when they prepare societies for war?

For anarchists, the answers do not begin with choosing which flag deserves our loyalty. The history of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries shows that nationalism has repeatedly been used to convince ordinary people that the interests of their rulers are their own. Workers who have more in common with each other than with their own governments are encouraged to see each other as enemies because states require obedience, sacrifice and the willingness to kill. The war in Ukraine is no exception. It is a conflict shaped by Russian imperial ambitions, Ukrainian nationalism, NATO expansion, Western strategic interests and the wider competition between global powers. The people trapped inside this struggle are paying the price for decisions made by governments that claim to represent them.

Sam Haines ended up fighting and dying as a volunteer militia as part of the Azov battalion that emerged in 2014 during the conflict in eastern Ukraine. Its early period was associated with individuals and organisations connected to far-right nationalist politics. Some of its founders had histories linked to ultranationalist movements, and the organisation used symbols and imagery that attracted criticism because of their associations with European fascist traditions. Scholars, journalists and human rights organisations have documented these connections. When Azov was incorporated into Ukraine’s National Guard, it became an official military unit rather than an independent militia. Some argue that integration changed the organisation and that its fighters have since played a significant role in defending Ukrainian territory. Critics sttae that formal incorporation does not erase its ideological origins or the influence that nationalist movements gained through wartime conditions. Denying or minimising the reality of these movements serves the interests of those who want war narratives to remain simple and unquestionable.

The uncomfortable truth is that states have often relied on extremist movements when those movements are useful. Governments that present themselves as defenders of civilisation have repeatedly made alliances with forces they would condemn under different circumstances. During wartime, groups willing to use violence are often granted influence because military effectiveness becomes more important than political principles. This pattern is not unique to Ukraine. It has appeared throughout history wherever states have faced crises and sought to mobilise society around national struggle. The machinery of war creates conditions where authoritarian ideas can grow because war rewards hierarchy, obedience and the belief that violence can solve political problems.

The debate around NATO’s role in Ukraine is another area where discussion is often reduced to slogans. One side argues that NATO is a defensive alliance whose support for Ukraine is a necessary response to Russian aggression. The other argues that NATO expansion after the collapse of the Soviet Union created a security crisis that helped produce the conditions for war. An anarchist analysis should be sceptical of both state narratives because both begin …

author: Corey Oakley
title: Victorian Socialists launch statewide election campaign
content:
The following is the text, edited for clarity, of a speech by Victorian Socialists secretary Corey Oakley at the party’s state election campaign launch on Saturday, 1 August. The launch, held at the Aborigines Advancement League in the Melbourne suburb of Thornbury, was attended by around 800 party members and supporters from across the state. The party’s state election platform,

A socialist manifesto for real change,

was released at the launch—with the initial print run of 500 selling out on the night.

In the last year the Australian political map—as people here will know—has been turned upside down by the rise of One Nation in the polls. First, we saw them smashing the Liberal Party vote. And if you believe the polls that have been coming out over the past few months, they're now starting to smash into the Labor Party vote as well.

The election in Victoria in November is the first major statewide test of how far this development is going to go. And the outcome, I think, will define the terrain of politics across this country for years to come. 

It’s going to have huge ramifications for the election that’s happening in New South Wales in March next year, and the next federal election [due by May 2028]. All of those will happen in the context of what happens here in Victoria this year.

Now, we know that every step forward for One Nation is a victory for hatred, a victory for racism and for vicious right-wing politics. And we know that every step forward they take pushes the Liberal Party further to the right, further to attack migrants, and pushes the lunatic right wing in the media to demand even more extreme reactionary measures.

But we also know that the Labor Party offer no alternative that can galvanise people against the far right. They are incapable of advancing a vision of how society can be changed for the better.

How could the Labor Party do that? Labor is the party of genocide. It is the party of neoliberalism and privatisation, the party of attacks on the poor and the vulnerable. And the new Labor leadership in Victoria, whose education minister refused to give teachers the deal that they deserve and desperately need, is only going to take Labor further to the right.

So we cannot accept that those are the only options. What is desperately needed, and what we plan to provide, is a radical alternative that stands against the right, but also throws to the curb any idea that Labor’s corporate centrism can deal with the crisis our society is currently in.

We need bold socialist politics that identify and combat the key problem: that our society is ruled by and for the super-rich. And we need politics that stand against the racism and scapegoating that are at the core of the One Nation threat. We need a party that provides a vision of hope and solidarity, and stands for a radical redistribution of wealth and power in this state and in this country.

So that is why we are embarking today on the biggest socialist campaign this country has ever seen.

When we first set up Victorian Socialists in 2018, we stood just in the northern suburbs of Melbourne. For the last election in 2022, we ran across the west as well as the north—22 [lower house] seats altogether. This time we are running in every single seat statewide.

We have already preselected candidates in 72 lower house seats. That includes every seat in metropolitan Melbourne and more from across the state. We already have candidates in seats in Geelong, Bendigo, Ballarat and elsewhere. By the end of this month, we will have finalised candidates in every one of the 88 seats across the state.

Every voter in Victoria will have a socialist option to vote for, in both the lower house and the upper house. That is something that has never happened before, either in this state or anywhere else in Australia.

Now, running a statewide campaign is going to be an enormous undertaking. Since 2022, we’ve put extensive effort into building up our infrastructure and building up local organisation everywhere that we can, and we plan to expand that rapidly in the coming months. There are approximately 6,000 polling booths across Victoria that we will need to staff on election day. To do that, we’ll need at least 4,000 volunteers.

The people in this room are a crucial part of how we’re going to make that happen, which I’ll come back to.
